title: Deterministic polynomial-time construction of a prime of a given bit length
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that constructs a prime of every requested bit length in polynomial bit time?

The input is the unary string \(1^n\), for any integer \(n\ge2\). The output must be the binary expansion of some prime \(p\) satisfying
\[
2^{n-1}\le p<2^n.
\]
The prime may be any one in this interval; no particular choice, such as the smallest prime, is prescribed.

With the finite machine model and output predicate below, the precise assertion is
\[
\exists A\ \exists C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ 
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\quad
\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,1^n,y,Cn^k)
\land \operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)
\bigr).
\]
One fixed deterministic program and one polynomial bound must work for every requested length. This retains the source's unary-input prime-construction question and makes its bit-computation convention explicit.
definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge2\), the unary string \(1^n\) consists of exactly \(n\) consecutive copies of the symbol one. Its length, rather than the binary length of the integer \(n\), is the input size. Valid inputs are precisely these strings; other input strings impose no requirements.

A positive integer \(p\) is prime when \(p\ge2\) and every positive integer dividing \(p\) is either one or \(p\) itself. A binary output string \(y=y_0y_1\cdots y_{n-1}\) of length \(n\), with \(y_0=1\), represents
\[
\operatorname{val}(y)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}y_i2^{n-1-i}.
\]
Here each symbol \(y_i\) is identified with the integer zero or one. The predicate \(\operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)\) means that \(y\) has exactly this length, its first bit is one, and \(\operatorname{val}(y)\) is prime. No leading zeros, additional bits, compressed description or separate certificate form part of the output. This predicate is equivalent to requiring the ordinary binary expansion of a prime in the displayed interval.

An algorithm \(A\) is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with one read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes, and a binary output stream. Its finite control, finite tape alphabets and number of tapes are fixed independently of the input. Tape cells have nonnegative integer addresses. Initially all heads are at cell zero, work tapes are blank, the input tape contains the input followed by blanks, and the output is empty. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes the finite control, writes at most one symbol on each work tape, moves each head left, right or not at all by at most one cell, and appends at most one bit to the output. A move left from cell zero leaves the head there. The transition rule is a finite deterministic table, defined on every nonhalting state and tuple of scanned symbols, and a designated halt state ends the computation.

One transition costs one bit-computation step. All computation, preprocessing, reading and writing count, including production of all \(n\) output bits. There are no random bits, quantum operations, oracle calls, input-dependent advice or unbounded integers with unit-cost operations. The finite program may contain fixed constants, but receives no additional information depending on \(n\).

The predicate \(\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,x,y,T)\) means that the computation on input \(x\) reaches its halt state after at most \(T\) transitions and has produced exactly the finite output string \(y\). Requiring positive integer constants \(C,k\) expresses ordinary polynomial time: increasing them covers any fixed polynomial bound. Both constants and the whole finite program precede the universal quantifier over \(n\). The assertion is unconditional; an unproved hypothesis about primes or computational hardness is not an additional assumption.

context_blocks.text: The MFCS 2018 paper explicitly asks whether a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm can output an n-bit prime from the unary input specifying n. It distinguishes this construction task from deterministic polynomial-time primality testing and from probabilistic prime generation.

The 2022 survey formulates deterministic prime construction for every bit length at least two and explains its relationship with short time-bounded descriptions of primes. This card retains that all-length construction requirement and specifies the complete finite bit model.

The revised Chen–Lu–Oliveira–Ren–Santhanam manuscript proves an unconditional polynomial-time randomized algorithm that outputs a fixed prime with high probability for infinitely many requested bit lengths. Its Corollary 1.2 is a pseudodeterministic result: it permits random choices and does not give the deterministic construction required here.

The same manuscript records an unconditional deterministic upper bound of \(2^{(1/2+o(1))n}\) time, still exponential in the requested bit length. Its discussion of conditional polynomial-time construction uses stronger unproved hypotheses, including Cramér’s prime-gap conjecture; these are not assumptions of this card.

why: Prime generation is a canonical example where recognizing a suitable object is efficiently possible but constructing one deterministically remains unresolved. A positive answer would remove randomness from this basic number-theoretic construction at every bit length. A negative answer would establish an unconditional computational lower bound for a concrete total search problem. The connection with succinct descriptions of primes also makes the question central to research on derandomization and time-bounded information.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated existence assertion or of its full logical negation.

A positive answer must supply one finite deterministic program \(A\) and positive integers \(C,k\), and prove for every \(n\ge2\) that it halts on \(1^n\) within \(Cn^k\) bit steps and outputs exactly the binary expansion of an \(n\)-bit prime. The output prime need not be the first prime in its interval.

A negative answer must prove
\[
\forall A\ \forall C,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\quad
\exists n\in\mathbb N_{\ge2}\quad
\neg\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\ast}\ 
\bigl(
\operatorname{HaltWithin}(A,1^n,y,Cn^k)
\land \operatorname{PrimeOutput}(n,y)
\bigr).
\]
Thus each proposed deterministic program and polynomial bound must fail at some length, which may depend on both. Failure includes running longer than the bound, never halting, or producing an invalid prime output. This does not assert that some bit length contains no prime.

A randomized or pseudodeterministic construction, success only at infinitely many lengths, or a bound that is polynomial in the numerical value of the output instead of its bit length does not establish the positive assertion. A conditional result establishes the target only if its additional hypothesis is also proved. A lower bound for one search procedure does not establish the unrestricted negative assertion. This is an exact algorithm-existence question, so numerical \(1/100\) approximation is not a substitute for the required proof.

sentences: Given a requested bit length in unary, the task is to output the ordinary binary expansion of a prime with exactly that many bits.
The question asks whether one fixed deterministic algorithm can do this for every length at least two in polynomial bit time.
Primality testing is efficiently possible, while deterministic construction of a suitable candidate remains a central explicit-construction problem.
Polynomial-time pseudodeterministic generation is known for infinitely many lengths, but that algorithm still uses randomness and does not meet the all-length deterministic requirement.
A complete Lean answer must prove the existence of the required algorithm or prove that every deterministic program and polynomial bound fail at some requested length.

Read PDF pp. 1–2: its main model is oracle query complexity and its results are quantum pseudodeterministic separations/speedups. It cites the prime-construction result as background and does not give an all-length classical deterministic bit algorithm. Irreducible-polynomial construction, factoring modulo many primes, prime counting, and prime-gap bounds were kept distinct from the target. No verified resolution of the retained target was found; this is a bounded status review, not exhaustive proof of openness.

Uniformity is one finite machine before every input length, without advice, random choices or oracle access. Fixed finite tape alphabets and tape counts cannot hide an input-dependent table. Requiring positive integer C and k is equivalent to the previous positive-real-constant polynomial existence convention by enlarging the constants; this changes no algorithm-existence target. Ordinary multitape finite-bit conventions are polynomially intersimulable, and all output/preprocessing work is charged. Unary n is source-supported; time polynomial in n is not time polynomial in log n.

The output is any actual n-bit prime, not necessarily the smallest prime and not a succinct program for one. The negative quantifiers range over every program and polynomial bound, with a defeating input length allowed to depend on both. The negation is an algorithmic impossibility statement, not a claim that primes fail to exist at some length, and a counterexample to one proposed generator is insufficient.

The historical consolidated TCS-5930 reference is preserved without reopening inactive/archive material. No semantic duplicate consolidation or new relation is proposed by this inert review. The exact mathematical question remains a yes/no existence target; numerical approximation tolerance does not replace prime output or the full Lean proof.
